#4167. 10 Best Romance Anime Where Falling in Love is the Easy Part

Usama Mehmood is a Senior Writer at DualShockers with more than five years of experience in the video game industry. He has been writing professionally since 2021 and covering games since 2022, with work spanning guides, lists, reviews, and features across action-adventure games, JRPGs, open-world titles, racing games,

The romance genre in anime is evidently meaningful and important to countless fans, myself included. From obsessively reading Horimiya (better than the butchered anime) to bawling my eyes out at the peak that was Clannad and then its After Story.Most romance anime also have a habit of making falling in love look like the hardest part of a relationship. After several episodes of awkward encounters, stolen glances, misunderstandings, and finally working up the courage to confess, you'd think the two lovebirds had overcome their biggest obstacle.

If you're tired of dumb misunderstandings and love polyhedrons, here are some Romance Anime for People Who Hate Cheap Drama.

However, the real work begins after that phase. You see, feelings can be mutual, but that doesn't mean two people automatically know how to navigate each other's insecurities, conflicting personalities, or the unexpected challenges that life throws their way. Thankfully, some romance anime understand that there's considerably more to love than the excitement of a first confession.So, armed with my extensive cult following of this genre since my teenage years, here are the best romance anime where falling in love is the easy part, from one-off slice-of-life seasonals to the more emotionally demanding dramedies.

For all my fellow video gamers, I thought I’d reel you in with My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999. Getting over a breakup is never easy; I can attest to that, but Akane Kinoshita definitely wasn't expecting to find her next romantic interest through an online RPG.After discovering that her bf has been cheating on her, she meets Akito Yamada, a notoriously indifferent MMO gamer who initially seems uninterested in anything outside his favourite hobby. Their clashing personalities couldn't be more different, but their friendship gradually develops into something considerably more meaningful.

It’s a 13-episode show that beautifully explores emotional maturity and the importance of understanding another person rather than simply expecting them to reciprocate your feelings. The only downside I have to mention is that the anime doesn’t fully cover the story, so you might need to binge the manga to get the full experience here.

As someone who originally read the manga on and off on his phone, “I Have a Crush at Work” (2025) stayed on my radar as soon as I heard it was in production. Workplace romances are complicated enough without having to pretend you're not dating the person sitting a few desks away.But then you have these two coworkers, Yui Mitsuya and Masugu Tateishi, who start a relationship but decide to keep it secret from their colleagues. That arrangement, in turn, creates an amusing contrast between their professional behaviour and how they act together when nobody is around them.

Fair warning: It’s a little more comedy-based, but beneath that layer, the show neatly tackles a relatable problem: how do you maintain a healthy relationship when you spend so much of your day together, yet can't openly acknowledge it? And that’s exactly where this show will make you adore it wholeheartedly.

We’re keeping the Workplace Romance streak going, and this is the perfect time to give some appreciation to one of my and everyone else’s all-time favorites in this sub-genre of romance anime: Wotakoi.I genuinely think it needs little introduction, given how widely popular it is, whether it's the show or even the web manga. Two adults who are hopeless romantics in theory, but who actually have absolutely no idea how to navigate an actual relationship? This show literally answers that question with childhood friends, Narumi and Hirotaka.

And not just them; you also get a healthy dose of screen time with their respective co-workers, and if I’m being honest, I may slightly prefer Hanako and Kabakura’s cute moments to the two main characters. But again, we’re in a similar problem where the anime and OVAs don’t fully adapt everything, so either go read it or, like me, hopelessly wait for a follow-up season.

Like what My Happy Marriage has to offer? Well, here are some of the best shows that feature somewhat of a similar theme.

This next one’s from my nostalgic vault because, like Wotakoi, Golden Time is a popular romcom anime that’s beloved by (almost) everyone. You’ve got a fairly simple premise at the beginning: our MC, Banri Tada, is settling into college life when Kouko barges in, and the two fall for each other quickly.And that’s the easy part. The bigger elephant in the room is that Banri has lost the memories of his hometown and past after an accident, and the real kicker is what that gap does to a relationship once the honeymoon glow wears off.

What I like is how mature the drama feels between these two characters and the rest of the cast, especially at a time when I thought all romance anime felt the same, with their usual high school settings. The show obviously isn’t a masterpiece or anything, but if you want an anime where the feelings are the easy part and the baggage drives most of the plot, it’s worth the 24 episodes.

We’re taking things old-school here, back to the golden age of the late 2000s, when the shoujo series Itazura na Kiss aired. Look, a lot of romance anime are happy to wrap things up once the two leads finally get together, but this show gives you a broader look than your typical lovey-dovey couple story.It follows Kotoko and Naoki from their school days into adulthood, showing how their relationship changes as they navigate college, marriage, and just life in general beyond their adolescence.

Now, given that it is based on a 1990s Shoujo, Naoki’s behavior and character may be slightly concerning, but trust me, the show is genuinely a wholesome treat, especially when these two start living under one roof, getting through their daily frictions of life, and then eventually build a family together.

TONIKAWA, or rather, as I prefer to call it, Tonikaku Kawaii, is easily one of the sweetest romcoms I had the pleasure of reading long before the seasonal anime adaptation premiered.What’s so great here is how the show totally skips the confession part: Nasa meets Tsukasa, falls for her, and they then get married very early in the story. From there, the series focuses on the joys and growing pains of newlywed life, as the pair learn more about each other while adjusting to living together.

It's honestly a bit more lighthearted than you’d expect from the other entries I’ve mentioned here, but oh man, I’d be lying if I didn’t mention how almost every single moment of these two puts a gigantic smile on your face. Apologies in advance to any hopeless romantics out there, but trust me, this show is a massive ball of sunshine to help cheer you up.

Falling in love for the first time is one thing, but then figuring out how to make that relationship work is an entirely different challenge.It’s a universal experience almost all of us go through when we’re young and full of these different aspirations. Yet Tsuki ga Kirei captures that awkward transition beautifully through Kotaro Azumi, an aspiring novelist, and Akane Mizuno, a track-and-field enthusiast, who grow closer during their final year of middle school.

Their relationship begins with these little tender yet familiar moments, but the show doesn't treat getting together as the finish line. Instead, it explores everything that comes afterward with jealousy, parental expectations, and the looming uncertainty of moving on to high school. It's a sincere coming-of-age romance that understands exactly why staying together can be harder than falling in love.

These 7 romance anime capture the quiet moments that linger long after the credits roll, perfect for when your heart needs a little extra love

My days of avidly consuming manga or watching almost every interesting anime in my piled-up backlog on MAL/Kitsu are long gone, but when a show like “You and I Are Polar Opposites” comes along, it instantly reminds you why this medium is still alive and kicking for you.It quite literally lives up to the title: on one hand, you have Suzuki, an energetic and sociable high school girl; on the other, you have Tani, her quiet, straightforward classmate who’s just the epitome of the silent-treatment energy at first glance. Despite their contrasting personalities, they develop feelings for each other and eventually take the plunge, starting a relationship.

And it’s not just about them; you get to see their everyday lives grow together alongside their wildcard cast of friends/classmates. It has those high school romcom tropes going for it, but trust me when I say the writing and character dramedy are exceptionally well done, and almost every episode feels like a joy to watch, with no filler.

Nana is one of my favorite anime and manga series of all time. I’ve got Nana Osaki as my avatar across most of my socials, and it's mainly because of how much this show means to me. What starts as a story about two young women navigating life in Tokyo slowly becomes one of the most emotionally complex explorations of love, friendship, and heartbreak I've ever experienced.

The series doesn't romanticize the idea of finding someone and living happily ever after; instead, it showcases two bittersweet parallels: Hachi's search for affection and stability, which often leads her into situations that make her question her own worth, while Nana's fiercely independent exterior hides a vulnerability she struggles to confront.I sometimes obsess over Ai Yazawa's writing in this series because nobody feels entirely innocent or irredeemable; almost all of these flawed young adults make messy decisions, hurt people they care about, and occasionally sabotage their own happiness.

To some of you reading, I hope you can relate to me on one thing: there’s some media you just can’t revisit with all earnestness because it’s left an emotional scar.That’s exactly what Clannad: After Story did to me, and I both love and hate it for doing that. While the original Clannad does a wonderful job establishing Okazaki and Nagisa's relationship, After Story takes things several steps further by exploring what happens once the sunshine of adolescence is over. It’s also where the show takes a full-blown descent into heartbreak.

The two are no longer simply teenagers; they're young adults trying to figure out what it means to build a life together. Marriage, parenthood, financial struggles, grief, and letting go. That one entire episode dedicated to Okazaki realizing and forgiving his Father has absolutely scarred my heart.The overall show and the OG VN are important to a lot of fans in the medium, almost being iconic for how the story beats were presented in it, like a train wreck. It's a bittersweet yet painfully gut-wrenching narrative, and one I still find hard to revisit without getting a lump in my throat.

Love isn’t always simple, but these 7 best romance anime on Crunchyroll capture its magic, heartbreak, and everything in between.

Share your take with fellow players. Keep it constructive, relevant, and respectful.

#4166. Holiday Gift Guide 2026

With the holiday gift-giving season upon us, it’s time to think about the gaming fans in your life and find the ideal present to brighten their day. And if you’re the gamer in the family, we always encourage you to circle relevant items in the coming pages and leave your magazine open in hard-to-miss locations around the house. We’ve scoured dozens of tech products, tabletop games, collectibles, and more to select and highlight some of the coolest items we found this year.

We recommended the Board shortly after its launch, but with its expanded game library and lower price than first-adopter rates, this holiday season is an ideal time to make the leap. This family-friendly platform features original games that sit comfortably between the digital and physical divide. The horizontally placed screen shows the backdrop of one of the several included games, or the sold-separately add-on games that have popped in since launch. Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. New subclasses, spells, creatures, magical items, and factions add thoughtful, intriguing options for both players looking to play someone new and DMs hunting for new story hooks and challenges. $50

If you’re as excited as we are about this month’s celebration of the Tomb Raider legacy (see p. 40), this centerpiece statue is an ideal fit for your collection. Standing roughly nine inches in height, Lara is poised for exploration in her original classic garb. The sculpt strikes a perfect balance between crisp detail and stylistic presentation, in line with that early version of the character; the metallic blue motorcycle paint is especially striking. $250

For players longing for the glory days of stand-up arcade games, it’s hard to beat Arcade 1Up’s approach. The team’s sturdy cabinets look and sound great as a marquee feature of your game room. The new Outrun machine features much of the original display art, a bright 19-inch screen, and responsive gas and brake pedals as you steer around those tight corners. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.

#4165. T1 brings TenZ out of retirement a day after re-signing crashies from Fnatic

T1 has added two-time Masters champion Tyson 'TenZ' Ngo to its Valorant roster for VCT Pacific in 2027. The move ends his retirement and builds on T1's signing of crashies, who has just left London-based Fnatic.

T1 has ended Tyson ‘TenZ’ Ngo’s retirement. The organisation confirmed on 12 November that he will join its Valorant roster for VCT Pacific in 2027. It made the announcement with a post and a welcome video.

T1 called him a ‘living legend’ of Valorant. It said he was starting a new chapter with the organisation.

TenZ retired from professional play in 2024. He has spent this year at T1 as a content creator. The announcement moves him from that role into the competitive squad.

His record explains the attention. With Sentinels, he beat Fnatic 3-0 in the Masters Reykjavík 2021 final. He then won Masters Madrid 2024 with a 3-2 win over Gen.G. That made him the first Americas player to win more than one VCT Masters event, Liquipedia records.

The TenZ news came a day after T1 confirmed Austin ‘crashies’ Roberts. He returns six years after T1 released him in September 2020. crashies called T1 the place ‘where it all started’. He said he was excited for the new challenge.

He played for Fnatic from 11 December 2024 until 4 November 2026. He joined T1 on 11 November 2026.

T1 has also kept some continuity. It extended BuZz’s contract on 6 November 2026. The new deal runs until the end of 2028.

The VCT structure for 2027 was announced on 28 October. Under it, the eight Pacific partner teams go straight into Kickoff in January 2027. The other four Kickoff places go to teams from regional open qualifiers.

#4161. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

#4160. Dota 2 returns to Esports World Cup 2027 as PARIVISION chase a first repeat title

Dota 2 will return to the Riyadh-hosted Esports World Cup in 2027, though dates, format and prize money are still to come. The title has never been won twice, and its prize pool has fallen at every edition so far.

Dota 2’s place at Esports World Cup 2027 was announced without dates, a prize pool, a format or any invited teams. The whole event is listed for July to August 2027.

The 2026 tournament had originally been planned for Riyadh before it was moved to Paris on 20 May 2026.

The first edition, Riyadh Masters 2024, carried a US$5,000,000 prize pool. In 2025 Team Spirit took US$1,000,000 from a US$3,000,000 pool in a 16-team event. The 2026 tournament ran from 7 to 19 July with 24 teams. That field was eight teams larger than a year earlier.

The winner still takes a large share. PARIVISION collected US$750,000, or 37.5% of the pool, plus 1,000 Club Championship points. Runners-up BetBoom Team received US$340,000 and 750 points, Liquipedia reported.

Those points feed into a larger prize. In 2026 the Club Championship paid US$30 million across the top 24 clubs. The champion club received US$7 million from an overall event prize pool of US$75 million. AG.AL won it with 5,300 points, stopping Team Falcons from winning a third title in a row. For organisations weighing the cost of a Dota 2 roster, that club prize is part of the calculation.

Not every club is staying. Falcons released all five players from the roster that won The International 2025, according to Timesaver.gg.

No club or player has won the event’s Dota 2 title more than once. Each of the three editions went to a different club with a different roster. Gaimin Gladiators beat Team Liquid in the 2024 final. A year later, Team Spirit swept Team Falcons 3-0. As the 2026 champions, PARIVISION now get the first chance to defend the title.

PVISION are your Dota 2 at EWC26 Champions! 👏 pic.twitter.com/34U67Oaj7G

— Esports World Cup (@EWC_EN) July 20, 2026

Their rivals arrive in form. Team Spirit went out of the 2026 event before the final. A month later, they won The International 2026 in Shanghai. Yatoro and Collapse became the first players to win three Internationals. Team Yandex finished third at both the 2026 Esports World Cup and The International. After signing ATF, they won PGL Wallachia Season 9 and BLAST SLAM VIII.

The route into the event is taking shape. The organiser’s Road to EWC qualifier programme for 2027 aims to involve 1.8 million players across more than 400 events. Qualifier slots for each game will be announced later. Counter-Strike 2, already confirmed for both 2027 and 2028, will hold a 32-team event in Riyadh from 20 July to 1 August 2027.

#4158. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4157. Heartopia surprise launches on Steam and shockingly, everyone seems to be happy

Heartopia players didn't actually end up having to wait too long to play the game on Steam, which is certainly not what anyone expected.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

#4155. MSI 2027 heads to Valencia as Riot reshapes Split 1 with First Stand: All In in China

Riot will take the Mid-Season Invitational to Spain in 2027, bringing a top-tier League of Legends event back to Europe for the first time since the Worlds 2024 final in London. Its one-off, expanded First Stand in China will also change Split 1 for the LEC, with the full details due in January.

Europe will host a top-tier League of Legends event again in 2027. Riot set out its international calendar on 13 November, the eve of the Worlds 2026 final. The Mid-Season Invitational goes to Valencia. London’s staging of the Worlds 2024 final was the last time the continent held an international League of Legends tournament.

For British fans, that puts a top-tier event within Europe next year. Riot has not yet given dates or ticket details for the Feria de Valencia event.

Spain’s last international League of Legends event came in 2019. That year, Madrid’s Palacio Vistalegre staged the Worlds quarter-finals and semi-finals. Valencia has never hosted one before.

China will stage First Stand: All In at the start of the 2027 season. Riot calls this single edition its largest tournament ever.

First Stand 2027 had originally been given to Southeast Asia. The bigger format took it to China instead. Southeast Asia will now host the event in 2028.

The change reaches every regional league, including the LEC. The larger event will change Split 1, just as Fnatic, G2 and the other LEC teams rebuild their rosters. In 2026, First Stand ran from 16 to 22 March, between the two regional splits. A bigger event at the start of the year leaves less certainty about how that window will look in 2027.

Riot has not yet said how many teams will take part or how they will qualify. Until then, LEC teams are building squads without knowing how many European places are on offer.

Worlds 2027 will be shared between two countries. The Swiss Stage goes to Nagoya, Japan. The quarter-finals and semi-finals move to the Suwon Convention Center in South Korea. The title decider goes to Seoul Arena, which is still under construction.

The arena was 81% built on 23 October. Work is due to finish in May 2027, with the venue opening in June 2027.

The city is backing the event with public money. Seoul has set aside 1.369 billion won (about US$1.02 million) in its proposed 2027 budget to host the Worlds final and Fan Fest, Sheep Esports reported.

#4154. 10 Best Indie Video Game Boss Fights of 2026

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Year after year, indie video games constitute an increasingly significant portion of the best experiences the interactive medium has to offer, regardless of your favorite genre.

Whether you prefer horror, action-adventure, or RPGs, especially when it comes to niches like boss rushes or Metroidvanias, the ever-reliable indie developers are always ready to satisfy your gaming needs.

For the past couple of generations, I've personally focused more on these kinds of products than on big-budget blockbusters because I find them more exciting, which allows me to talk about them at length.

So, to start wrapping up the year and reflect on the great adventures we've enjoyed—and be warned that there will be spoilers for the games mentioned below—here are the ten best indie video game boss fights of 2026.

As a fan of games that simply throw memorable enemies at you with no filler in between, Gurei was one of my most pleasant surprises of 2026.

The idea of creating a boss rush where the foes vary in difficulty and complexity depending on the order in which you choose to face them, also affecting the abilities you have at your disposal, is fascinating, and this is most evident when you face the Beetle Kami.

This force of nature is an enjoyable fight, whether it's your first or last encounter, as it perfectly embodies the kind of battles that rely on learning precise movement patterns, leaving no room for error if you want to emerge victorious.

In all my Gurei runs, I rarely dared to leave the Beetle for last because the ability it gives you is powerful, but also because its difficulty spikes dramatically. In any case, it's clear that all his versions offer a satisfying clash between two honorable warriors, which is the best kind of duel.

Kernel Hearts is a game I admire more for its story and soundtrack than its gameplay. However, its bosses are the exception, especially thanks to the presence of entities like God.

Fighting at the edges of reality with an immortal being that constantly changes shape and name becomes fascinating in a matter of seconds, particularly because of its strange fighting style that perfectly explains why it's the deity of the game's world.

It's a grueling two-phase encounter that demands meticulous control of positioning and attack windows, all while avoiding beams of light, giant cubes, spiritual representations of your teammates, and the constant onslaught of its divine claws.

Like any good roguelike, the power level you reach when facing the final boss is what truly determines how much you'll suffer, but whether it's easy or difficult, God offers a magnificent fight.

As we approach the midway point of 2026, let's take a look at some under-the-radar indie gems that already feel like cult classic video games.

While Replaced didn't quite live up to my expectations, I wholeheartedly consider it among 2026's best action games, with The Commissioner being the greatest showcase of its precise gameplay.

Specifically, the second encounter with Cole Carpenter exploits all the title's mechanics to their fullest potential, forcing you to dodge, parry, and shoot as the situation demands in order to keep up with him.

The burning environment and tense soundtrack also perfectly complement the encounter, which highlights the magnificent animations and choreography that Replaced brings to its simple yet visually stunning combat system.

Overall, the game's roster of main enemies is good, but due to its narrative weight, audiovisual presentation, and elegant flow, The Commissioner is undoubtedly the most memorable one.

Well Dweller dedicates its entire campaign to pitting you against terrifyingly well-designed enemies in incredibly creative fights, eventually pairing you with The Queen so you can free your family (and the kingdom) from her yoke.

Striking the face of this abject royalty as you watch her gradually deform is a stunning sight, even when you're too busy dodging her countless projectiles to notice that you're slowly revealing her true form.

After hours of honing your skills and learning to maneuver Glimmer, Well Dweller tests your ability to jump, dodge, glide, and bounce without pausing for a second, forcing you to be so precise that you'll only succeed if you enter a state of flow.

Unlike the bosses in most modern Metroidvanias, which are heavily influenced by the Soulsborne philosophy, The Queen belongs to the more traditional action-platformer formula, and that makes her sensational.

Hack and slash games have been on the decline for many years, which is quite a shame for those of us who are fans of great fights, yet sporadically we get gems like SoulQuest that remind us of the genre's greatness.

Despite being conceptually simple, the way it adapts the gameplay style to two dimensions is compelling, as is the showdown against Morrigan, a feast of visual spectacle and stylized mechanics that fully exploit the title's strengths.

With all your combos and abilities unlocked, it's not just that you tackle a fast and multifaceted boss that attacks in numerous ways and directions, but also the fact that you can particularly counter them with a plethora of magnificent moves, fully settling the power fantasy.

Defeating a good boss is satisfying, but doing so with a deliberate use of interconnected attacks for diverse purposes to push your style metric to the limit is much more, so we have to thank SoulQuest for bringing back Devil May Cry's magic.

If you are feeling nostalgic, take a look at these 10 best boss fights of the PS1 era.

Never underestimate how much an excellent presentation can elevate the experience of a boss fight, especially when you have examples like the final encounter with Dolores in Crisol: Theater of Idols.

Thanks to her stunning art design, fighting her leaves you completely captivated, but even more so when you notice the Resident Evil inspiration behind the encounter, based on methodical positioning and remarkable aim to target her weak points.

Furthermore, the emotional component also plays a significant role because, without going into detail to avoid spoilers, the dialogues that unfold during the confrontation are heartbreaking, providing a powerful conclusion to the game's compelling story.

Crisol: Theater of Idols perfectly captures the essence of the genre's greats while forging its own unique identity, and it's impossible to finish the campaign with this fight and not be convinced of its remarkable quality.

Future Knight is, without a doubt, among the most original experiences I've had in 2026, and the fight against the Lady from the Past is just the icing on the cake of a game that only needs three hours to win you over.

Although all the bosses are bizarre and incredibly fun in their own way, finally facing the leader of the cult that brainwashed the world is special thanks to all the layers of the skirmish.

Facing an elderly woman who throws bombs from her hands, summons tiny old men who shoot everywhere, hurls flying underwear at you, and fires glitched paintings while distracting you by counting sheep is not the kind of memory that fades easily.

The secret boss in Future Knight would also be a strong contender for this distinction, though I'm sticking with the Lady from the Past because I still laugh when I think about her, thanks to how improbably entertaining the fight was.

One of the main reasons I believe MIO: Memories in Orbit belongs on the list of the best Metroidvanias of all time is its roster of bosses, with Shii leading the pack due to everything that her encounter entails.

The final challenge that separates you from the true finale is precisely the entity that has accompanied you throughout the journey, proving to be an incredibly powerful being that perfectly showcases the game's dynamic approach to boss fights.

Between its teleportations, position changes, rapid charges, variety of attacks, and diverse projectiles, it's a clash that compels you to use every tool at your disposal, making positioning just as crucial as knowing when to dodge.

If you add to that the ending it gives you access to, the lore of its background, and the remarkable soundtrack that accompanies it, Shii becomes the ultimate icon of MIO: Memories in Orbit, which is saying a lot considering the existence of fights like those of Ati, Sol & Vin, and Nabuu.

These 10 Easy But Impactful Boss Fights prove that challenging encounters aren't always needed to be a memorable boss

Boss fights in horror games are highly functional but also linear in their execution, unless your name is Tenebris Somnia and you deliver a confrontation as impressive as Lacuna's.

All the bosses in the game boast incredible design, both in pixel art and FMV, but this one in particular is a string of gameplay and visual surprises that keep you amazed until the very last second.

Honestly, I want to keep descriptions to a minimum to preserve the element of surprise, yet I will say that it's among the most incredible bosses in the entire genre for how it uses the environment, story, and mechanics to create a sense of being in front of an actual supernatural force.

It's true that combat isn't Tenebris Somnia's strong suit, but bosses like Lacuna know how to overcome limitations and turn their simplicity into a strength, as it allows you to focus on the fight's terrifying and immersive exhibition.

Mina the Hollower is a game that will surely be remembered as one of the finest in the entire indie scene of this decade, as it exudes such generational quality that every sequence is a masterpiece.

Nevertheless, facing Baron Lionel in his various forms is the campaign's clear highlight, boasting such inventive gameplay that you'll want to lose on purpose just to have another chance to fight him.

Whether in his standard form, which you face in the typical fashion the game has offered so far, or in his radiant form, which takes full advantage of the glorious tower-climbing mechanic to add verticality and perpetual movement to the fight, you'll be so satisfied that you won't want to fight any other boss for a good while.

Divine pixel art, superb music, an entire narrative sequence that defines the campaign's plot twist and reveals its treacherous nature, two independent phases that exploit the best of each of the game's gameplay facets... Yes, Baron Lionel is the whole package, and perhaps even more.

Thus, the most villainous villain in Mina the Hollower stands as the best indie video game boss fight of 2026, as it is also the best written, the best presented, and the best visualized of all the contenders.

If you want to catch up on the best releases of the year so far, I recommend the ten best indie games of 2026 (so far).

#4153. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4152. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4150. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4147. All Heists Ranked in GTA Online

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

With the newest installment of GTA on the horizon, some players are wondering what they might be able to expect from a new GTA Online mode if it comes about. The biggest and best draw for GTA Online was the major heists that made players really feel like a career criminal.

While some players may enjoy simply running a criminal enterprise in San Andreas, many are hoping to see some new and engaging heists appear in GTA VI. It may not be far off but it can always be important to remember where you started when you get where you’re going.

For that reason this list will encompass all eleven heists, counting the Doomsday Heists as three individual heists, and rank them from worst to best. A lot of what makes heists so much fun is how different they are and how they can appeal to some very different styles of play.

Of all the heists in GTA Online The Prison Break Heist is arguably the odd man out compared to a lot of the others. As one of the original heists added during the heists update back in 2015, it’s definitely been played enough for players to come to a decision about it.

Unless you were coming prepared with a team who knew what they were doing this heist could get very annoying very quickly. While prison breaks may be a popular trope in movies it seems that it’s not quite as popular to participate in.

Added to the roster of heists in 2017 this is the first part of the three part heist in which players are introduced to the Doomsday storyline and meet the eccentric cast of characters. As contractors the players will attempt to stop an attack on government servers.

The heist is pretty good, but being the first of the overall storyline means things really only get better from there. This puts a bit of a damper on the heist itself as it's really a precursor to some much better and more interesting heisting.

When your very favorite insane person shows up and asks you for help establishing a drug running operation you’re obligated to help. That’s pretty much the whole premise for this heist and even with Trevor’s wild personality it doesn’t exactly hit the highs of the other heists.

The biggest issue is that the finale simply isn’t as interesting as many others, since it’s entirely about defending a position from waves of attackers. Many players enjoy what Trevor brings to the table but the heist doesn’t close itself out well enough to satisfy.

Rockstar is adding official support for GTA Online roleplay and plans to reveal more details September 8.

The very first original heist opened up the floodgates for players to enjoy an all new way to play GTA V. With just one other player, you were tasked with helping Lester on a small job to rob Fleeca Bank before making your getaway in the Kuruma.

Since it is the introductory heist, it stays relatively grounded and simple. That isn’t a bad thing, but when compared to the other heists it just doesn’t stand up despite the feeling of nostalgia the heist gives players.

As the second part of the Doomsday Heist things start to get a little more interesting with this heist. Players will find themselves investigating a Russian submarine to uncover a crazy conspiracy and engage in some underwater infiltration.

The memorable setting and story do a lot of the heavy lifting for this heist before the inevitable finale which earns it a stronger reputation. Unfortunately, the prep for this one isn’t as engaging as some putting it a bit lower on the list.

The most recently added heist having been added in 2026, The Kortz Center Heist is a classic old school Art Job. Scout the museum, figure out the best way past security and make off with some very pricey paintings.

One of the few heists that you can complete solo gives it a major boost, but also becoming an art thief is incredibly cool. The big issue here is that you won’t get even close to being able to do this heist until you’ve managed to wrack up enough cash for a mansion with an Art Studio.

This is a detailed list that goes over games similar to GTA that are perfect to play while waiting for GTA 6.

Another of the original heists, The Humane Labs Raid is an intricate and entertaining heist that sees players engage in a bit of serious Seal Team Six work. Players will infiltrate a secret research facility to steal data after activating an EMP to go in under the cover of dark.

One of the standouts of the original heists, it really nails the feeling of infiltrating a secret facility. The finale is pretty incredible but many would argue that the setup missions are tedious though that doesn’t stop it from being a favorite amongst the originals.

The final culmination of everything the Doomsday Heist has been building and the payoff is well worth it in every sense. Players will be attempting to stop the true Doomsday Scenario, but with a bit of a twist that we’ll leave for now just in case you haven’t played it yourself.

Arguably one of the most challenging finales of all of the heists, this one really puts you in the shoes of an action hero as you fight your way through the heavily armored enemies. That’s also what makes it a little divisive given how difficult the finale can be.

This heist, introduced in 2020, was the first heist to allow players to complete it entirely solely earning it a lot of leeway in terms of appreciation. Breaking into a fortified private island of a drug lord in a lot of different ways certainly helped too.

Many people adored it for being completeable solo, and earned it a good reputation since you no longer had to rely on others for help. Some did have things to say about the prep missions and overall stealth mechanics of the heist.

GTA 6 Online could arrive sooner than expected, according to the Twitch CEO.

The Pacific Standard Job is the culmination of the first line-up of heists added to GTA Online. Players prepare themselves to rob the Pacific Standard Bank in a true and classic heist that really encapsulates what GTA Online heisting is all about.

There’s no denying that of all the heists in the game, this one evokes that sense of being a career criminal better than any other. With the actual job being an incredible experience and the getaway being a particular high point.

At the very top of this list sits the most interesting heist in the whole game added way back in 2019, The Diamond Casino Heist. Players break into the Diamond Casino in a few different ways and make off with tons of cash from the casino in a truly epic fashion.

With three different kinds of entries, all of which are incredible, there’s a good amount of flexibility in how to approach it. Each entry has its own perks but all are memorable and really make you feel like you stepped into a casino heist movie.

The PUBG x PAYDAY Streamer Challenge begins May 13th for PC, and May 21st for console.

#4146. Talking Point: What's Your Favourite Tiny Tweak In Zelda: Ocarina Of Time?

While the Ocarina of Time we see on Switch 2 is undoubtedly the same game we all know from the N64, there are enough tweaks in there that have had the biggest fans amongst us clicking and pointing at the screen like that Leonardo DiCaprio meme.

We're not talking about the big changes, either. You can keep your new visuals, fancy jump buttons and modern camera controls; we're getting excited over new floor textures and wall decals — stuff that wouldn't stand out unless you had played the original more times than you care to admit.

Below, we have shared our favourite tiny tweaks that have stood out so far. Some are more niche than others, but these are the little changes that had us beaming in our first few hours of rediscovering Hyrule and finding it not quite as we remember it.

After you've read through our picks, why not head to the comments and share your top tweaks?

Editor's Note. If there's any Zelda-related topic (or, indeed, anything else game-related) you'd like to bring to the attention of NL and the community, remember you can also submit letters for our monthly letters page. The mailbox is looking per-ritty empty at the time of writing, and we'd wager it's down to a certain November game keeping you all occupied!

Knowing the original game like the back of my hand, I'm yet to walk into a room without going, "Oooh, look how they changed that bit!" But the one that has stood out to me the most so far is being able to ride Epona right up to the entrance to Kakariko Village without getting chucked off at the bottom of the stairs.

Does it change the game in any way at all? Absolutely not. But praise be to whichever innovative dev at Nintendo thought, 'What if Jim didn't have to sit through a backtracking animation every time he forgot to dismount quickly enough?'

The ragdoll may not be a substantial inclusion, but if I can pick between a stiff, canned animation of Link collapsing to the floor and seeing his lifeless body tumble into the rapids that lead up to Zora's Domain, you know what I'm going to choose.

The option to remove one of the few tweaks I haven’t enjoyed so far — Navi’s incessant dialogue boxes commenting on everything — is a godsend. I was concerned she’d spend the entire game puncturing the mood with “Oooh, big mountain!” and “Wow, great work!” and “OMG, that was a lucky escape!” (I’m paraphrasing, but that’s the gist), and she does.

Turning on the ‘Master’ display option, though, reduces the UI to the bare minimum, removing almost everything, including Navi’s dialogue boxes. So when I emerge onto Hyrule Field, the landscape speaks for itself (with a little help from the music). Bliss. Other people might enjoy her interjections, and yes, I will miss a cute line or two, but thanks for letting me turn off the running commentary, Nintendo.

Turning Grouch Mode off, the slingshot easter egg in the courtyard window is ace. And Kakariko feels more like a real place now. And those little rivulets on Hyrule Field add so much. And that part of Lon Lon... *babbling trails off...

Without heading into spoiler territory, I suppose my niche tweak (if it’s considered niche) would be the addition of Threads of Time, but more specifically the Tapestry.

I’ve filled out my tapestry now, but throughout each stage of Link’s journey it was nice to see the progress I was making. I jumped into the remake with the hope of experiencing it with fresh eyes (although I’d played the original), and it really felt like it at times. It was also a really good way for me to gauge what I could do next should I forget, collectables I likely still needed, or even secrets I still had to unlock.

It’s a very simple addition common in modern gaming, but a tweak which was needed.

I’m enjoying all the revamped music, but one arrangement that took me by surprise is when you encounter common or garden foes. There’s more urgency and danger now: notes are sharply cutting in, there’s a subtle, unnerving rise and fall in volume, and if the battle lasts long enough, it goes up a notch when a horn (I’m guessing!) is eventually layered on top.

For a track I hadn’t given a second’s thought to in the original, I’m now delighted every time an enemy nears.

Note. Very minor pre-Hyrule Field spoilers ahead...

Some of the subtle tweaks to Ocarina of Time’s narrative landed so well with me. I won’t go into the later examples, but I absolutely adored the moment when Link runs into both Mido and Saria after leaving the Deku Tree.

Mido, who feels much more fleshed out in the remake, expresses shock and immediate concern for the Deku Tree, while Saria is devastated at the thought of Link leaving Kokiri Forest. She leaves, heartbroken at Link’s decision, and it’s only when we exit the forest that she catches up to make amends and deliver the Fairy Ocarina.

This extra scene isn’t much in the grand scheme of things, but it really adds weight to Link’s departure, emphasising the home and friends that he’ll be leaving behind. I love it.
